newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina to fire "Blond Angel" spy - reports.
newsitem.headline: Argentina to fire "Blond Angel" spy - reports.

text.p: An embarrassed Argentine government has ordered its navy to fire from the intelligence service an officer wanted in France for human rights abuses and murder, newspapers reports said on Thursday.

The French government accused Argentina on Wednesday of double-crossing it after the navy admitted Capt. Alfredo Astiz -- known as the "Blond Angel" for his one-time choir boy looks -- still worked in its intelligence service.

"I ordered (Navy Chief Adm. Carlos) Marron not to asign any other function to Astiz in the navy," Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez told the Clarin newspaper in Paraguay, where he was attending a meeting of the Mercosur customs union.
Dominguez added that President Carlos Menem had been unpleasantly surprised by the news that Astiz was still working with the navy.
"We didn't know anything about it," Dominguez said. La Nacion newspaper carried a similar report.
An unnamed cabinet member told Clarin that "the news fell on Menem like a bucket of cold water."
A Defence Ministry spokesman in Buenos Aires said he could not confirm Dominguez's remarks.
Astiz became a hated symbol of military immunity from punishment for murder, kidnapping and torture under the 1976-83 dictatorship.

Tried and sentenced after democracy returned, but freed under an amnesty for "Dirty War" officers in 1989, he was forced to retire late last year after a campaign by human rights groups and pressure from France.

Astiz, 46, was sentenced to life in jail in France in absentia for the murder of French nuns Leonie Duquet and Alice Domon in 1977. Sweden also wants to try him for the disappearance of Swedish teenager Dagmar Hagelin.
All three are believed to have been killed at the Navy School of Mechanics (ESMA), the military junta's most infamous torture centre.
Argentina refuses to extradite Astiz, who also walked free from a court-martial for alleged cowardice in the 1982 Falklands War with Britain.
At least 10,000 people disappeared during the military campaign of terror against leftist guerrillas during the rule of the juntas.
